questions.question: What does it mean for $\boldsymbol x_0$ to be an adherent point of $\boldsymbol E$?
options: Every ball $\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x_0,\varepsilon)$ intersects $\boldsymbol E$ nonemptily.
Some ball around $\boldsymbol x_0$ avoids $\boldsymbol E$, no matter which values are selected.

questions.question: How is the closure of $\boldsymbol E$ described using closed sets?
options: As the intersection of all closed sets containing $\boldsymbol E$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, is $0$ an adherent point of $(0,1)$?
options: No, because $(0,1)$ has no adherent points.
Yes, but only for balls of radius exactly $1$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, is $2$ an adherent point of $(0,1)$?
options: Yes, every point of $\mathbb{R}$ is adherent to $(0,1)$.
No, because only $0$ can be adherent to $(0,1)$, under all circumstances whatsoever.
No, a sufficiently small ball around $2$ does not intersect $(0,1)$.

questions.question: Why can an isolated point of a set still be an adherent point of that set?
options: Because each ball around it intersects the set at least at that point itself.
Because adherent points must be different from the candidate point.
Because isolated points are always outside the closure.
Because closure ignores the original set.
